Spells in Turkey, Egypt, Belgium and India saw him chase the football around the world deep into his thirties, and France capped him 80 times, with a runners-up medal from the 2006 World Cup as a teammate of Zidane and co.

footballers.name: Dimitri Payet
clues: I was born on the 29th of March 1987. I played 38 times for my country, scoring 8 goals.
I was in the team of the tournament at UEFA Euro 2016, reaching the final.
I was in the PFA Team of the Year in 2016, despite not playing for one of the biggest clubs.
I had two spells at Marseille with a Premier League stint in between.
I scored a free kick for West Ham so good that the opposing manager applauded me on the touchline.
footballers.story: A late bloomer who became, for one extraordinary season, the most exciting player in the Premier League. Payet's 2015-16 at West Ham was full of free-kick wonder goals and ridiculous assists, earning him a place in the PFA Team of the Year and a starring role at Euro 2016 on home soil, where he scored against Romania in the opener. Twice a Marseille player, he had two great spells at the Velodrome either side of the West Ham fairy-tale. His exit from London, where he downed tools to force a return to France, soured the legacy but cannot dim the football.

footballers.name: Daley Blind
clues: I was born on the 9th of March 1990. I played 99 times for my country, scoring 2 goals.
I got to the semi-final of the 2014 World Cup, before being signed by the same manager for a Premier League club.
I could play left-back, centre-back, or sit in front of the back four, and managers loved me for it.
I won three Eredivisie titles before I left, and another one when I came home a decade later.
I spent four seasons at Old Trafford before going home to Ajax in 2018.
footballers.story: Footballing brain, footballing surname. Daley Blind played anywhere Ajax or Manchester United needed him: left-back, centre-back, defensive midfield, all with the same calm distribution learned from his father Danny. He won the Eredivisie multiple times at Ajax, played a key role in the 2014 World Cup semi-final run, and lifted the 2017 Europa League at Old Trafford. A heart condition diagnosed in 2019 ended for many but not him; he carried on, returning to Ajax to win another title, then taking a Bayern Munich loan and a stint at Girona.

footballers.name: Sami Hyypiä
clues: I was born on the 7th of October 1973. I played 105 times for my country, scoring 5 goals.
I won a cup treble in my second season in England, lifting the FA Cup, League Cup and UEFA Cup in one summer.
My country never qualified for a major tournament throughout my long international career as captain.
I formed a formidable centre-back partnership with a future Sky Sports pundit.
I won the Champions League final in Istanbul.
footballers.story: Liverpool's £2.6m bargain of the century. Houllier signed Hyypiä from Willem II in 1999 and got a decade of commanding, almost serene centre-back play in return. He was central to the 2001 cup treble and lifted the Champions League in Istanbul in 2005, one of the great captain's nights even if Gerrard wore the armband. Bayer Leverkusen gave him a Bundesliga sign-off, and he later managed them. Finland never reached a major tournament with him, which remains a small injustice given how much he carried that defence.

footballers.name: Stewart Downing
clues: I was born on the 22nd of July 1984. I played 35 times for my country, scoring 0 goals.
I played in a UEFA Cup final for my hometown club, losing to Sevilla in Eindhoven in 2006.
I joined Liverpool in 2011 for around 20 million pounds and endured a famously rough first season under Kenny Dalglish.
I returned to Middlesbrough for a third spell, helping the club back into the Premier League.
England fans will remember me from Euro 2012, where I played every minute of the group stage on the right wing.
footballers.story: A proper old-school English left winger whose career felt like a barometer of the early Premier League boom. Stewart Downing came through at Middlesbrough, helped them to a UEFA Cup final in 2006, and earned a big move to Aston Villa before Liverpool spent £20m on him in 2011, a deal that defined the post-Torres anxiety on Merseyside. He rebuilt at West Ham, looked like a genuinely top-class creator again, and finished by helping Boro back to the Premier League. Quiet, technically sound, and frequently underrated.

footballers.name: Fabien Barthez
clues: I was born on the 28th of June 1971. I played 87 times for my country, scoring 0 goals.
At one point I was the most expensive goalkeeping transfer in British football history.
I won the European Cup with Marseille.
I won both the World Cup and the European Championship with my country.
I won the Premier League in my first season at Manchester United.
footballers.story: The bald, charismatic Frenchman who won a Champions League at 21 with Marseille and never quite stopped being unpredictable. Fabien Barthez moved to Monaco, then Manchester United for a world-record fee for a goalkeeper, where his sweeping and ball-playing dazzled before the howlers crept in. He returned to France with Nantes, lifted the 1998 World Cup with Zinedine Zidane kissing his head for luck, and added Euro 2000 for good measure. Retirement brought a second career in motor racing, because of course it did.

footballers.name: Jermain Defoe
clues: I was born on the 7th of October 1982. I played 57 times for my country, scoring 20 goals.
I'm one of only a handful of players to score 150 plus goals in the English top flight.
I was one of those players that Harry Redknapp kept signing.
I formed one of the classic big-man-little-man partnerships with Peter Crouch.
I left Tottenham twice and came back twice, which says something about my feelings for the place.
footballers.story: A poacher's poacher who refused to fade away. Jermain Defoe burst out of West Ham, infamously biting Javier Mascherano along the way, then scored goals everywhere he went: two spells at Tottenham, Portsmouth, a Sunderland relegation fight that he very nearly won single-handed, Toronto, Bournemouth, and finally Rangers in the SPL. He finished with 162 Premier League goals. Above all that statistical noise sits his friendship with young Sunderland fan Bradley Lowery, an act of footballing love that endeared him to the country far beyond his goals.

footballers.name: David Villa
clues: I was born on the 3rd of December 1981. I played 98 times for my country, scoring 59 goals.
I top-scored at Euro 2008 with four goals, then had to watch the final from the bench after picking up an injury in the semi.
I won silverware in Spain with Valencia, Barcelona and Atlético Madrid.
I won the Champions League in my first season at the Camp Nou.
I am still my country's all-time top scorer, and I lifted the World Cup wearing the number 7 shirt.
footballers.story: Spain's all-time top scorer. El Guaje rose at Sporting Gijon, exploded at Valencia, then moved to Barcelona where he won La Liga, the Champions League and just about everything else under Guardiola. He scored five goals at the 2010 World Cup as Spain were crowned champions, and he had already won Euro 2008. Atletico Madrid gave him a famous final La Liga title in 2014 as Simeone's outsiders broke the duopoly. He finished up in MLS with NYCFC and at Vissel Kobe in Japan, scoring everywhere he went. A pure, ruthless centre-forward.

footballers.name: Henrik Larsson
clues: I was born on the 20th of September 1971. I played 106 times for my country, scoring 37 goals.
I won the Champions League, setting up both goals against Arsenal.
I played for Manchester United in a brief loan spell in 2007.
I was a prolific scorer in the United Kingdom, but not in the Premier League.
I scored for Sweden in the 1994 World Cup third-place match.
footballers.story: From stacking fruit in a Helsingborg warehouse to seven seasons of unrelenting goals at Celtic, 242 of them, Henrik Larsson built one of the great underrated careers. Feyenoord launched him; the Hoops adored him. A move to Barcelona at 32 brought a Champions League winner's medal in 2006, and the famous Thierry Henry line that "people speak about Ronaldinho and Eto'o but I think Larsson won the final". A loan stint at Manchester United enchanted Old Trafford, and he ended back at Helsingborg, eventually playing alongside his son Jordan.

footballers.name: Darren Bent
clues: I was born on the 6th of February 1984. I played 13 times for my country, scoring 4 goals.
I scored a goal that deflected in off an inflatable beach ball and the referee gave it.
In the 2009-10 season I scored 24 league goals, roughly half of Sunderland's total for the entire campaign.
I was a striker who played for Charlton, Tottenham, Sunderland and Aston Villa, scoring effectively at every one of them.
I was frequently close to making England squads for major tournaments but never made the final cut.
footballers.story: An English centre-forward who was steadily, unfussily excellent for the best part of a decade. Darren Bent came through Ipswich, banged them in for Charlton, then traded up to Tottenham, Sunderland (for a then-British record from Wearside), Aston Villa, Fulham, Brighton and Derby. He scored 106 Premier League goals despite playing for almost every mid-table side. He will, inevitably, always be the man whose deflected shot off a beach ball beat Pepe Reina at the Stadium of Light in 2009, the most ridiculous goal of the Premier League era.

footballers.name: Andrey Arshavin
clues: I was born on the 29th of May 1981. I played 75 times for my country, scoring 17 goals.
I became Arsenal's most expensive signing in history at the time of my arrival.
I scored four goals in a game.
I had a feud with a manager over fitness and weight which the tabloids loved to cover.
My number-23 shirt at Arsenal sold in huge numbers in Moscow the summer I signed.
footballers.story: The cheeky, broad-shouldered Russian who briefly lit up the world. Andrey Arshavin won the UEFA Cup with Zenit Saint Petersburg in 2008, then danced through Euro 2008 as Russia reached the semi-finals, drawing every big club in Europe. Arsenal got him for a club-record fee and, on a wild April night at Anfield, he scored four against Liverpool in a 4-4 draw. The brilliance was sporadic after that. He drifted back to Zenit, then Kuban, and finally Kairat in Kazakhstan, the smile never quite leaving him.

footballers.name: Joleon Lescott
clues: I was born on the 16th of August 1982. I played 26 times for my country, scoring 1 goal.
I lifted the Premier League trophy on the last day of the 2012 season.
My move to Merseyside in 2006 took a few seasons to convince the locals, but I left as a fan favourite.
I was hit by a car as a five-year-old and left with a fractured skull, but recovered to become a professional footballer.
I was bought by a Manchester club in a late-summer 2009 saga that involved my old club lodging a tapping-up complaint.
footballers.story: The defender who, as a child, was hit by a car and was told he might never play again. Lescott came through at Wolves, then established himself in the Premier League at Everton under David Moyes, where he was one of the best ball-playing centre-backs in the country. Manchester City paid big money in 2009 and he won two Premier League titles in the early Sheikh Mansour years, including the famous Aguero campaign of 2011-12. West Brom and Aston Villa rounded things off, and 26 England caps tell their own story.

footballers.name: Dwight Yorke
clues: I was born on the 3rd of November 1971. I played 74 times for my country, scoring 19 goals.
I formed one of the most famous striking partnerships in Premier League history.
I scored 17 league goals in a single season at a Midlands club, then doubled my haul in red after a club-record move.
I scored in both legs of a Champions League semi-final against Juventus, including a header in Turin that helped turn the tie.
I won the treble in 1999 at Old Trafford, and my goal-of-the-month against Arsenal in the FA Cup semi-final still gets replayed.
footballers.story: That smile. Yorke was the laid-back genius of Manchester United's 1999 Treble, forming a telepathic partnership with Andy Cole that fired them to the Premier League, FA Cup and Champions League in one of football's great seasons. He had emerged at Aston Villa under Graham Taylor and Brian Little, where his pace and finishing made him a Villa Park favourite. Blackburn, Birmingham, Sunderland and a fondly remembered spell at Sydney FC followed, where he was the marquee signing of the inaugural A-League. Forever Trinidad and Tobago's most famous footballer.
footballers.numbers: 19 goals in 74 caps for Trinidad and Tobago

footballers.name: Jamie Carragher
clues: I was born on the 28th of January 1978. I played 38 times for my country, scoring 0 goals.
As a child I supported the biggest local rival of the team I went on to play for my entire career.
I have scored seven own goals in my Premier League career, the second-most in the competition's history.
I retired from international football, then called into talkSPORT to push back at a pundit's criticism of me.
I played in two Champions League finals in three years, winning one and losing the other to a Milan side I'd already beaten.
footballers.story: A Bootle-born Evertonian who became one of Anfield's most decorated lifers. Jamie Carragher made over 700 appearances for Liverpool, all heart and positional intelligence, never quite quick but always in the right place. He was the cramping, defiant figure who refused to lose in Istanbul 2005, dragging Liverpool through a Champions League final that should not have been possible. FA Cups, League Cups and a UEFA Cup followed. Since hanging up the boots he has become Sky's sharpest analyst, the scouse half of the country's most quoted punditry double act.

footballers.name: Tomáš Rosický
clues: I was born on the 4th of October 1980. I played 105 times for my country, scoring 23 goals.
I won two FA Cups at Arsenal, although injuries restricted my appearances over a decade in north London.
I won the German League title in 2002.
I captained the Czech Republic at Euro 2012.
I scored a memorable volley against Sunderland in 2013 for Arsenal that won the Premier League goal of the season.
footballers.story: Little Mozart. Tomáš Rosický conducted Sparta Prague as a teenager, won the 2002 Bundesliga with Dortmund, and then spent a decade at Arsenal where his vision, scampering runs and Theatre of Dreams strike against Spurs lit up the rare seasons his hamstrings allowed. Injuries cost him whole years of his prime, but he never lost the elegance or the smile. He returned to Sparta to finish where he began, and remains the most-capped Czech outfield player of the modern era.
footballers.numbers: 23 goals in 105 caps for Czech Republic

footballers.name: Ricardo Carvalho
clues: I was born on the 18th of May 1978. I played 89 times for my country, scoring 5 goals.
Jose Mourinho once suggested I should take an IQ test, after I publicly questioned why he hadn't started me in a season opener.
I was named UEFA Club Defender of the Year in 2003–04.
I've been managed by Jose Mourinho at three different clubs.
I was stamped on by Wayne Rooney at the 2006 World Cup — he was sent off for it.
footballers.story: The most underrated centre-back of his generation. Won the Champions League with Porto, the Premier League three times with Chelsea, La Liga with Real Madrid — and Euro 2016 with Portugal at 38. Wherever Mourinho went, Carvalho followed.
footballers.numbers: 19 club goals in 433 appearances · 89 caps for Portugal
didYouKnow: Followed José Mourinho from Porto to Chelsea in 2004, then again from Inter to Real Madrid in 2010 — one of the great manager-player partnerships of the era.
Retired from international football in 2011 saying he'd been "disrespected", then came back nearly three years later and won Euro 2016 with Portugal at 38.
Was given a seven-month suspended prison sentence in Spain in 2017 for tax fraud during his Real Madrid years — a fate that befell several Spain-based stars of his era.

footballers.name: Cheick Tioté
clues: I was born on the 21st of June 1986. I played 52 times for my country, scoring 1 goal.
I represented my country at the 2010 and 2014 World Cups, and the 2012 and 2013 Africa Cup of Nations.
I scored arguably the most famous goal in my club’s modern history — a stunning volley to make it 4–4 against Arsenal, completing a comeback from 4–0 down.
I played alongside Yohan Cabaye and Hatem Ben Arfa in a midfield that gave Newcastle their best Premier League finish in years.
I tragically collapsed and died during a training session in June 2017 at the age of 30.
footballers.story: A warrior in the truest sense — Cheick Tioté played football like every tackle was a matter of honour. The Ivorian arrived at Newcastle from FC Twente in 2010 and quickly became the heartbeat of Alan Pardew's midfield, a ferocious ball-winner whose energy and aggression set the tone for everything the team did. His volley against Arsenal in February 2011 — completing a comeback from 4–0 down to draw 4–4 — remains arguably the greatest goal in Newcastle's modern history. He was part of the Ivory Coast squad at two World Cups and was capped 52 times. His death during a training session in China in June 2017, aged just 30, shocked the football world. Tyneside has never forgotten him.
honours: Africa Cup of Nations runner-up (Ivory Coast, 2012)
footballers.numbers: 1 goal in 52 caps for Ivory Coast
didYouKnow: His volley to make it 4–4 against Arsenal in February 2011 — completing a comeback from four goals down — is widely regarded as the greatest goal in Newcastle's Premier League history
He formed a formidable midfield partnership with Yohan Cabaye that powered Newcastle to fifth place in the 2011–12 season
He tragically collapsed and died during a training session with Beijing Enterprises in China in June 2017, aged just 30

footballers.name: Mauro Icardi
clues: I was born on the 19th of February 1993. I played 8 times for my country, scoring 1 goal.
I was once the top scorer in Serie A, finishing ahead of Gonzalo Higuaín and Edin Džeko.
Despite being one of the most prolific strikers in Serie A, I was barely capped by my country — largely due to off-pitch controversies.
I moved to Paris for around €50 million but was never the first-choice striker, spending much of my time on the bench.
I married the ex-wife of a former teammate — a scandal that dominated Italian football gossip for years.
footballers.story: One of the most prolific — and most controversial — strikers of his generation. Icardi was a clinical finisher who scored over 120 goals for Inter Milan, captaining the club and finishing as Serie A's top scorer in 2014–15. But the drama was never far away. His relationship with Wanda Nara — the ex-wife of former teammate Maxi Lopez — became one of Italian football's biggest soap operas and alienated him from dressing rooms and national team selectors alike. Despite his goalscoring record, Argentina capped him just eight times. A €50 million move to PSG in 2020 promised a fresh start, but he spent most of his time behind Mbappé and Neymar. A career defined equally by goals and gossip — few players have divided opinion so sharply.
didYouKnow: He was stripped of the Inter Milan captaincy in 2019 after a bitter contractual dispute that saw him frozen out of the squad for months
His marriage to Wanda Nara — the ex-wife of his former Sampdoria teammate Maxi Lopez — created one of Italian football's most infamous off-pitch scandals
Despite scoring over 120 goals for Inter, he won just 8 caps for Argentina — one of the most prolific strikers ever to be virtually ignored by his national team

footballers.name: Michael Essien
clues: I was born on the 3rd of December 1982. I played 59 times for my country, scoring 9 goals.
My teammates nicknamed me ‘The Bison’ because of my extraordinary physical power.
I won two Premier League titles, three FA Cups, a League Cup, and was an unused substitute in my club’s Champions League final victory.
My transfer to the Premier League cost £24.4 million, making me the most expensive signing in my new club’s history at the time.

I scored a spectacular late equaliser against Arsenal that was voted my club’s Goal of the Season. Two years later, I struck an unforgettable left-footed volley from 25 yards in a Champions League semi-final against Barcelona.
footballers.story: The Bison — a nickname that perfectly captured the raw, bulldozing power of one of the most complete midfielders the Premier League has seen. Essien arrived at Chelsea from Lyon for a then club-record £24.4 million in 2005 and became the engine room of Jose Mourinho’s dominant side. He could tackle like a defender, run like a sprinter, and shoot like a striker — his thunderous volley against Barcelona in the 2009 Champions League semi-final remains one of the great European goals. Knee injuries robbed him of his best years, and loan spells at Real Madrid and AC Milan saw diminishing returns. He finished his career with stints at Panathinaikos and Persib Bandung, far from Stamford Bridge — but at his peak, few midfielders on the planet could match him.
didYouKnow: His teammates nicknamed him The Bison because of his extraordinary physical power and ability to charge through midfields
His left-footed volley against Barcelona in the 2009 Champions League semi-final is widely regarded as one of the greatest goals in the competition's history
His £24.4 million transfer from Lyon in 2005 made him the most expensive African player in history at the time

footballers.name: Jimmy Bullard
clues: I was born on the 23rd of October 1978. I was called up to the England squad three times but never won a cap.
My career was plagued by knee injuries. I dislocated my kneecap after a tackle, missing 15 months. On my debut for my next club, I injured the same knee within 40 minutes.
Before turning professional, I worked as a painter and decorator while playing non-league football.
I was signed by West Ham, the club I supported, for just £30,000 — but never made a first-team appearance and was released on a free.
My career took me from non-league to the Premier League, from painting houses to playing at the highest level, but injuries meant I never quite fulfilled my potential.
footballers.story: The funniest man ever to play in the Premier League — and a genuinely brilliant footballer when his knees allowed it. Bullard worked as a painter and decorator while playing non-league football before West Ham signed him for £30,000, only to release him without a first-team appearance. Peterborough gave him a chance, and from there he climbed to Wigan, where he became one of the most creative midfielders in the division. A £2.5 million move to Fulham followed, and he was magnificent — but a horrific knee injury in 2006 robbed him of 15 months. Hull City paid £5 million for him and he repaid them with one of the greatest goal celebrations ever seen, recreating Phil Brown's infamous half-time team talk. Another knee injury on his Ipswich debut effectively ended his career. A cult hero and now a popular social media personality, Bullard is the ultimate what-if of English football.
footballers.numbers: 0 goals in 0 senior caps for England
didYouKnow: He worked as a painter and decorator while playing non-league football before turning professional in his twenties
His goal celebration at Manchester City — recreating Phil Brown's infamous half-time team talk by wagging his finger at his teammates in a circle — is one of the most iconic in Premier League history
He was called up to the England squad three times but never won a cap, with injuries always intervening at the worst moments

footballers.name: Kevin Phillips
clues: I was born on the 25th of July 1973. I played 8 times for my country, never scoring a goal.
I played for an extraordinary number of clubs across English football — more than most strikers could dream of.
I formed one of the Premier League’s great ‘little and large’ partnerships with a tall Irish target man — between us, we scored 77% of our club’s goals in one season.
I announced myself with a hat-trick in a 5–0 away win at Derby, during a season that saw me named Premier League Player of the Season.
In my greatest season I scored 30 Premier League goals — winning an award no Englishman has claimed before or since in the top flight of European football.
footballers.story: The only Englishman ever to win the European Golden Boot — and he did it at Sunderland, of all places. Phillips scored 30 Premier League goals in 1999-2000, forming a devastating partnership with Niall Quinn that fired the Black Cats to a seventh-place finish in their first season back in the top flight. Small, sharp, and ruthlessly clinical inside the box, he was the complete poacher. England somehow gave him only eight caps and never let him score. After leaving Sunderland he became a footballing nomad — Southampton, Aston Villa, West Brom, Birmingham, Blackpool, Crystal Palace, Leicester — racking up nine clubs in total, scoring goals at every single one. He scored the winning penalty in the 2011 League Cup final for Birmingham against Arsenal, one of the great cup upsets.
honours: Premier League Player of the Season (2000)
didYouKnow: He remains the only Englishman ever to win the European Golden Boot, scoring 30 Premier League goals for Sunderland in the 1999-2000 season
He played for nine different clubs across his career — scoring goals at every single one of them
He scored the winning penalty in the 2011 League Cup final for Birmingham City against Arsenal, one of the biggest cup upsets of the decade

footballers.name: Steve Bruce
clues: Around the turn of the century I wrote three football crime novels about a player-manager who solved murders.
As a manager I won four promotions to the Premier League, two with Birmingham and two with Hull.
I scored two late headers to beat Sheffield Wednesday in April 1993, a moment often credited as the birth of 'Fergie Time'.
I was a defender, yet I once scored around 19 goals in a single season, many from the penalty spot.
I lifted three Premier League titles and three FA Cups as a Manchester United defender and captain.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 31st of December 1960. I was never capped by my country.
footballers.story: Steve Bruce was Sir Alex Ferguson's rugged, fearless heartbeat at the back, a centre-half who hurled his head and body at everything and captained Manchester United to their first league title in 26 years. In 1994 he became the first English skipper of the 20th century to lift the Double, a broken-nosed embodiment of grit who somehow never won a senior England cap. When the boots came off he built a second life in the dugout, dragging Birmingham and Hull up through four promotions across a long, weathered managerial road. From Old Trafford talisman to hard-bitten journeyman gaffer, his story is pure, unglamorous English football.
didYouKnow: Despite captaining Manchester United to the Double, Bruce was never once capped by England at senior level, widely rated among the best English defenders of his era never to play for his country.

His two late headers against Sheffield Wednesday on 10 April 1993, the winner deep into stoppage time, swung the inaugural Premier League title toward United and are credited with coining the phrase 'Fergie Time'.

While managing Huddersfield in the late 1990s he wrote three football-themed crime novels, Striker!, Sweeper! and Defender!, which he later admitted embarrassed him but have since become cult collectors' items.

footballers.name: Wilfried Zaha
clues: I came through a London club's academy and made my debut for them as a teenager.
I am a fast, tricky winger whose whole game is running straight at defenders.
I earned a big-money move to Manchester United, but it did not work out.
I returned to my old club and became their long-serving talisman.
In 2023 I moved abroad and helped Galatasaray win the Turkish league title.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 10th of November 1992. I played 34 times for my country, scoring 5 goals.
footballers.story: Wilfried Zaha was Crystal Palace, a south London boy who joined at eight and grew into the heartbeat of Selhurst Park across two spells. Electric off either foot, he could beat a man in a phone box and terrorised Premier League full-backs for a decade, the fear factor every Palace game was built around. A big-money move to Manchester United promised the world but never took flight, and he came home to become a genuine club legend. Born in the Ivory Coast and raised in Croydon, he played twice for England before pledging his future to the country of his birth. Later he chased silverware abroad and finally lifted a league title with Galatasaray.
footballers.numbers: 5 goals in 34 caps for the Ivory Coast
didYouKnow: He was born in the Ivory Coast and raised in Croydon, and played twice for England before switching to represent the country of his birth.
A big-money transfer to Manchester United never worked out, and he returned to Crystal Palace to rebuild his career.
He is a long-serving Palace talisman who joined the club as a boy and starred across two separate spells at Selhurst Park.

footballers.name: Thiago Alcantara
clues: My father won the 1994 World Cup, and my brother played international football for a different country than I chose.
I won the German league title in every one of my seasons at that club.
I came through Barcelona's La Masia academy as a midfielder.
My time in England was badly disrupted by injuries.
I was a Spanish midfielder in the mould of Xavi and Iniesta.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 11th of April 1991. I played 46 times for my country, scoring twice.
footballers.story: Born in Italy to a Brazilian World Cup winner but shaped by Barcelona's La Masia, Thiago was a footballer of two touches and a thousand ideas. He glided through midfields as though the pitch tilted to meet him, a metronome who could slow a game down or split it open with a single disguised pass. Pep Guardiola prised him away to Bayern Munich, where he won the Bundesliga in every one of his seven seasons and, finally, the Champions League. A move to Liverpool followed, injuries nagging but the class never dimming. He played the game the way he saw it, unhurried and beautiful.
didYouKnow: His father, Mazinho, was part of the Brazil squad that won the 1994 World Cup in the United States.
He won the Bundesliga title in every one of his seven seasons at Bayern Munich.
He signed for Liverpool in September 2020, just weeks after lifting the Champions League with Bayern.

footballers.name: Titus Bramble
clues: I spent five seasons at Newcastle United.
In 2009 I was named Wigan Athletic's Player of the Year.
In 2006 I won the UEFA Intertoto Cup.
I built a cult reputation as a gifted centre back who was also prone to the odd costly error.
I played in the Premier League for Ipswich, Newcastle, Wigan and Sunderland.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 31st of July 1981. I was never capped by my country at senior level.
footballers.story: Titus Bramble was the kind of centre-back who kept you on the edge of your seat, for better and for worse. A big, quick, aerially dominant defender from Ipswich, he earned a move to Newcastle as a teenager when Sir Bobby Robson came calling, and he played Champions League nights in front of the Gallowgate roar. He never quite shook the reputation for the odd calamity, yet those who watched him closely knew the ability was real, the recovery pace genuine and the heart never in doubt. At Wigan he rebuilt his name and became a cult hero, voted the club's Player of the Year. Thirteen straight seasons in the Premier League tell you he was far better than the punchlines ever allowed.
didYouKnow: Newcastle signed him as a young centre-back from his hometown club Ipswich Town in 2002, with Sir Bobby Robson the manager who brought him to St James' Park.
He won the UEFA Intertoto Cup with Newcastle United in 2006, having scored a memorable volley against champions Chelsea to help secure European qualification.
He was voted Wigan Athletic's Player of the Year for the 2008-09 season after a run of commanding performances at centre-back.

footballers.name: Keylor Navas
clues: I have won La Liga, Ligue 1 and multiple Champions League titles.
More importantly, I also played for Nottingham Forest.
I have kept goal at three different World Cup finals.
At the great club of my career I won three European Cups in a row, a rare feat.
My country is no footballing giant, yet many call me the finest goalkeeper it has ever produced.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 15th of December 1986. I played 126 times for my country at the last count, without scoring.
footballers.story: For a boy from Perez Zeledon, the road to the top of the game ran a long way uphill. Keylor Navas made his name at Levante, then walked into Real Madrid and refused to be a passing footnote, keeping goal through three straight Champions League triumphs. In Costa Rica's shirt he became a national treasure, the goalkeeper whose flying saves carried a tiny nation to the 2014 World Cup quarter-finals. Paris came next, and a trophy-laden spell at PSG, before a late Premier League cameo on loan at Nottingham Forest. Small country, giant career.
footballers.numbers: 0 goals in 126 caps for Costa Rica
didYouKnow: He kept goal for Real Madrid through their three consecutive Champions League triumphs from 2016 to 2018.
His remarkable saves inspired Costa Rica to the 2014 World Cup quarter-finals, the best run in the nation's history.
Late in his career he joined Nottingham Forest on loan during the 2022-23 Premier League season.

footballers.name: Ruud Gullit
clues: I was a versatile player who could line up anywhere from sweeper to centre-forward.
At one point I was the world's most expensive signing, when I signed for an Italian giant.
As a player-manager I won the FA Cup, the first manager from outside Britain to do so.
I was one third of a famous Dutch trio that won back-to-back European Cups.
I was instantly recognisable for my dreadlocks.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 1st of September 1962. I played 66 times for my country, scoring 17 goals.
footballers.story: With dreadlocks flying and a stride that ate up the turf, Ruud Gullit played like a man built to do everything at once. He could defend, drive midfield or lead the line, all with the same unhurried grace. In 1987 he swapped PSV for AC Milan in a world-record deal and became the beating heart of Arrigo Sacchi's revolution, forming a fearsome Dutch trio with Marco van Basten and Frank Rijkaard. That summer of 1988 he captained the Netherlands to their only major title, heading them ahead in the Euro final. Later he reinvented himself again, this time in a suit, guiding Chelsea to silverware. Few footballers ever carried so many gifts so lightly.
footballers.numbers: 17 goals in 66 caps for the Netherlands
didYouKnow: When he won the 1987 Ballon d'Or he dedicated the award to the then-imprisoned Nelson Mandela, using football's biggest stage to protest apartheid.
He was one third of AC Milan's legendary Dutch trio alongside Marco van Basten and Frank Rijkaard, the spine of one of the greatest club sides ever assembled.
As Chelsea's player-manager in 1997 he became the first non-British manager to win the FA Cup, ending the club's 26-year wait for a major trophy.

footballers.name: Troy Deeney
clues: I am my club's record goalscorer in the Premier League.
I lost an FA Cup final to Manchester City.
I scored one of the most iconic last-minute winners in all of football history.
I spent years as the long-serving captain of an unfashionable club.
After retiring I became a television pundit and a newspaper columnist.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 29th of June 1988. I was never capped by my country.
footballers.story: Troy Deeney was Watford's heartbeat, a captain who led with his chest out and his sleeves rolled up, the kind of centre-forward defenders felt long before they saw. He bullied his way through the Championship and then proved he could do it in the Premier League too, becoming the club's all-time top scorer in the top flight. Broad-shouldered and fearless, he wore the armband like it was stitched to his skin, dragging Watford up divisions and to a Wembley final. A Walsall and Birmingham lad who found his true home at Vicarage Road, he became one of the most beloved figures in the Hornets' modern history. Blunt, brave and box-office, Deeney was Watford through and through.
didYouKnow: He is Watford's all-time leading Premier League goalscorer, with 47 top-flight goals for the club.
He once said beating Arsenal was about having 'a bit of cojones', a jab at the visitors' lack of fight.
His injury-time winner against Leicester in the 2013 Championship play-off semi-final is one of the most dramatic goals in English football history.

footballers.name: Javier Zanetti
clues: I have scored in a knockout World Cup tie against England.
I was famous for my durability, playing on at the top until I was 40.
I was my country's most-capped player until Javier Mascherano passed me.
I won five Serie A titles as a versatile, tireless full-back.
I was Inter Milan's long-serving Argentine captain who lifted the 2010 Champions League.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 10th of August 1973. I played 145 times for my country, scoring 5 goals.
footballers.story: They called him Pupi, and for nineteen seasons he was simply Inter. Javier Zanetti arrived from Argentina in 1995 and never left, racking up a club-record 858 appearances at right-back, left-back or wherever the team needed a metronome who never tired. He was the captain who lifted the 2010 treble under Mourinho, ageless legs still overlapping in a Champions League final at 36. For Argentina he became the country's most-capped man, yet the biggest stages somehow passed him by. One club, one heart, one flag pinned to the San Siro forever.
didYouKnow: He spent 19 seasons at Inter and holds the club's all-time appearance record with 858 games.
He captained Inter to the 2010 treble under Jose Mourinho, the first player to captain an Italian club to the Scudetto, Coppa Italia and Champions League in one season.
Despite being Argentina's most-capped player, he was controversially left out of the squads for both the 2006 and 2010 World Cups.

footballers.name: Rafael van der Vaart
clues: I lost a World Cup final.
I spent a few seasons in Spain playing for one of the biggest clubs in the world.
A late move on transfer deadline day took me to a London club in the Premier League in 2010.
I am Dutch, and I built my name as an elegant number 10 who liked to dictate the play.
I played for Tottenham Hotspur, scoring plenty in white before returning abroad.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 11th of February 1983. I played 109 times for my country, scoring 25 goals.
footballers.story: A left foot dipped in silk, Van der Vaart was the last of the classic Ajax number tens, running the side as its youngest captain while still barely out of his teens. He carried that elegance to Hamburg and then Real Madrid, before a deadline-day dash to Tottenham turned him into an instant White Hart Lane cult hero, all curled finishes and clever movement between the lines. For the Netherlands he was a fixture across a golden decade, wearing the armband in the 2010 World Cup final in Johannesburg. Grace, guile and a knack for the spectacular defined him.
footballers.numbers: 25 goals in 109 caps for the Netherlands
didYouKnow: After hanging up his boots he took up the game professionally as a darts player, even winning a match on the pro circuit.
A teenage prodigy at Ajax, he was named the first ever Golden Boy in 2003 and captained the club while still only 21.
A dramatic deadline-day move from Real Madrid in 2011 made him an overnight cult hero at Tottenham.

footballers.name: Shay Given
clues: I moved to Manchester City in 2009, just as their big-money era was beginning.
I reached two FA Cup finals with Newcastle in the late 1990s.
I was my country's number one at the 2002 World Cup, reaching the last 16.
I was the goalkeeper at the other end when Thierry Henry's handball knocked my country out of a World Cup.
I finished my international career second only to Robbie Keane in caps.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 20th of April 1976. I played 134 times for my country, without scoring.
footballers.story: Born in Lifford, County Donegal in 1976, Shay Given began at Celtic without ever breaking into the first team, then quietly built one of the finest goalkeeping careers these islands have seen. Twelve years at Newcastle United made him a St James' Park institution, a shot-stopper of cat-like reflexes who twice earned a place in the PFA Team of the Year. Later moves to Manchester City, Aston Villa and Stoke carried him deep into his forties. For Ireland he was a fixture across two decades, calm and dependable through World Cup nights and bitter heartbreak alike. Few kept goal with such longevity, and fewer still with such quiet grace.
footballers.numbers: 0 goals in 134 caps for Republic of Ireland
didYouKnow: With 134 caps he is the Republic of Ireland's most-capped goalkeeper of all time.
He came through the youth ranks at Celtic and was even named on the bench for an Old Firm derby, but never played a first-team game for the club.
He was the goalkeeper at the other end when Thierry Henry's handball set up the goal that knocked Ireland out of the 2010 World Cup play-off.

footballers.name: Faustino Asprilla
clues: I was sent home from the 1998 World Cup after falling out with my national coach.
I won two UEFA Cups and a Cup Winners' Cup with Parma in Italy.
On a famous European night I scored a hat-trick against Barcelona.
That hat-trick came on Newcastle's first Champions League home game, in a 3-2 win.
My arrival at Newcastle is blamed by some for their famous surrender of a big Premier League lead.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 10th of November 1969. I played 57 times for my country, scoring 20 goals.
footballers.story: Nobody quite knew what Faustino Asprilla would do next, and that was the whole point. Long-limbed and gloriously unpredictable, El Pulpo could drift through a game before conjuring a moment of pure mischief, then wheel away into a spinning somersault and double fist-pump. At Parma he became a European star, his flair lighting up a golden Serie A side, before Newcastle paid a fortune to bring that chaos to the Premier League. He was a maverick in an era of them, a forward who played on instinct and left defenders guessing. Few footballers have made unpredictability feel so much like joy.
didYouKnow: He scored a stunning hat-trick against Barcelona on Newcastle's first Champions League home night in September 1997, under Kenny Dalglish.
His signature celebration was an acrobatic somersault followed by a double fist-pump.
He was a key part of the great 1990s Colombia side, winning 57 caps for his country.

footballers.name: Robert Huth
clues: I never played club football in Germany, despite being a German international.
I am one of only a handful of men to win the English top flight with two different clubs.
I scored twice away at a title rival during one of football's greatest underdog stories.
I was born in the eastern half of a city that was divided at the time.
I partnered Wes Morgan at the heart of Leicester City's fairytale title-winning defence.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 18th of August 1984. I played 19 times for my country, scoring twice.
footballers.story: Robert Huth was the kind of centre-back forwards dreaded, a towering slab of a defender who cleared his lines with elbows out and asked questions later. A Berliner by birth, he crossed to Chelsea as a teenager and never once played senior football back home, learning his trade in the English game and winning back-to-back titles under Jose Mourinho. Spells at Middlesbrough and Stoke hardened him into a Premier League institution, but the miracle was still to come. At Leicester, well into his thirties, he became a cornerstone of the most improbable champions football has known, heading and blocking his way into folklore. Rugged, dependable and quietly beloved, he made unglamorous defending feel like an art.
didYouKnow: He is one of only a handful of players to win the English top flight with two different clubs, lifting it with Chelsea and then Leicester City.
Despite being a German international, he never played club football in Germany, moving from Union Berlin's youth ranks straight to Chelsea.
He scored twice away at Manchester City during Leicester's 2015-16 title run, a stunning brace in a 3-1 win that pushed the Foxes clear at the top.

footballers.name: Scott Parker
clues: As a boy of thirteen I appeared in a famous fast-food television advert, keeping a ball up in my family garden.
I was signed by Chelsea for £10 million, from another London club.
In 2011 I was voted the Football Writers' Footballer of the Year, even though my club was relegated that season.
That standout campaign came while I was captaining West Ham United.
Back in England as a manager, I won promotion to the Premier League through the Championship play-offs.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 13th of October 1980. I played 18 times for my country, without scoring.
footballers.story: Scott Parker was the heartbeat kind of midfielder, the one whose value never quite showed up on a scoresheet but was felt in every recovered ball and every yard covered. He came through at Charlton as a boy wonder and moved between the big names, Chelsea, Newcastle, West Ham and Tottenham, always the industrious engine rather than the marquee signing. His finest hour came in claret and blue, driving a doomed West Ham side with such heart that the writers crowned him their Footballer of the Year even as the club went down. Composed, brave and endlessly willing, he was the sort of player supporters trusted with the dirty work. When the boots came off, the tracksuit went on, and a new career in the dugout began.
didYouKnow: As a 13-year-old he appeared as a ball-juggling boy in a famous McDonald's television advert made for the 1994 World Cup.
He was voted FWA Footballer of the Year in 2011 even though his West Ham side were relegated from the Premier League that season.
He moved into management after retiring, winning promotion to the Premier League with Fulham and later leading Bournemouth up from the Championship.

footballers.name: Emmanuel Adebayor
clues: I am my country's all-time top scorer, though we have only ever reached one World Cup.
I had a loan spell at Real Madrid, winning the Copa del Rey.
I reached a Champions League final as a young striker with Monaco in 2004.
I scored for three fierce Premier League rivals: Arsenal, Manchester City and Tottenham.
After scoring against my former club Arsenal, I sprinted the length of the pitch to celebrate in front of their fans.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 26th of February 1984. I played 87 times for my country, scoring 32 goals.
footballers.story: Tall, powerful and blessed with a striker's swagger, Emmanuel Adebayor was one of African football's great entertainers. He arrived at Arsenal from Monaco and blossomed into a menace, his finest season yielding thirty goals and a place among the Premier League's most feared forwards. From there came Manchester City, Real Madrid and Tottenham, each stop lit by that same loping, unstoppable running. For Togo he was simply everything, the talisman who carried a small nation onto the world's biggest stage. Loved, loathed and never once ignored, he played the game his own gloriously theatrical way.
didYouKnow: He is Togo's all-time leading goalscorer, with 32 goals for the national team.
After scoring against Arsenal for Manchester City in September 2009, he sprinted the full length of the pitch to celebrate in front of his former club's supporters.
He scored Premier League goals for Arsenal, Manchester City and Tottenham Hotspur across his time in England.

footballers.name: Paolo Maldini
clues: I was a naturally right-footed player who spent most of my career on the left.
My shirt number was retired when I left, on the condition it could return for one of my sons.
I won five European Cups across three different decades.
I scored inside the first minute of a Champions League final, only to lose it on penalties after leading 3-0.
I captained my club for over a decade and won seven Serie A titles.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 26th of June 1968. I played 126 times for my country, scoring 7 goals.
footballers.story: One club, one number, one lifetime. Paolo Maldini slipped into the Milan first team at sixteen and did not leave for twenty-five seasons, playing the last of them at forty-one. He was a full-back who could have been a poet, gliding across to smother strikers before they knew the danger had arrived, then doing the same shift at centre-half a decade later. Five European Cups and seven Scudetti passed through his hands as captain, yet he lifted them with a calm that made greatness look like routine. Elegance, loyalty and an almost cruel sense of timing, all in the red and black.
honours: UEFA Champions League / European Cup (AC Milan, 1989, 1990, 1994, 2003, 2007)
didYouKnow: Three generations of Maldinis have worn the Milan shirt: father Cesare, Paolo himself, and sons Christian and Daniel.
He made his Milan debut at sixteen and played his final match at forty-one, spanning twenty-five Serie A seasons at one club.
Maldini graced four World Cups and three European Championships but never won either, and Milan retired his number 3 in his honour.

footballers.name: Ross Barkley
clues: Pundits once compared my pace and power to Paul Gascoigne.
I won a European trophy, lifting the Europa League in 2019.
I also had a Premier League season at Luton Town.
I came through the academy at Everton, my boyhood club, a local lad from Liverpool.
My big-money transfer took me from Merseyside to Stamford Bridge in 2018.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 5th of December 1993. I played 33 times for my country, scoring 6 goals.
footballers.story: Ross Barkley was Everton to the bone, a Liverpool boy who climbed through the academy and announced himself as English football's next great hope. Blessed with a low centre of gravity and the strength to ride challenges, he carried the ball upfield like few of his generation, drawing early comparisons to Paul Gascoigne. A move to Chelsea finally brought the silverware his talent deserved, an FA Cup and a Europa League among them. When the Premier League cooled on him he rebuilt in the south of France with Nice, rediscovering the swagger that first made him special before finding his way home again.
didYouKnow: He came through Everton's academy as a local Liverpool lad and was long tipped as English football's next big thing.
He won the Europa League with Chelsea in 2019, coming off the bench in the final in Baku.
Managers and pundits once likened his powerful, ball-carrying running to that of Paul Gascoigne.

footballers.name: Samuel Eto'o
clues: I later became the president of my country's football federation.
I am the only player to win the treble in consecutive seasons with two different clubs.
I was named African Footballer of the Year four times.
I moved clubs as part of a swap deal involving Zlatan Ibrahimovic.
I was a Cameroonian striker who starred for Barcelona and Inter Milan.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 10th of March 1981. I played 118 times for my country, scoring 56 goals.
footballers.story: Born in the bustle of Douala, Samuel Eto'o carried Cameroon's swagger onto every stage football could offer. Quick, ruthless and impossibly durable, he bullied La Liga defences at Barcelona before conquering Italy with Inter. He remains the only man to win the continental treble in back-to-back seasons with two different clubs, the deadly point of both Rijkaard's and Mourinho's finest sides. For his country he was simply irreplaceable, the striker who lifted the Nations Cup twice and Olympic gold in Sydney. Loud, proud and forever an Indomitable Lion.
didYouKnow: He is the only player to win the continental treble in back-to-back seasons with two different clubs, taking it with Barcelona in 2009 and Inter Milan in 2010.
Eto'o was named African Footballer of the Year a record four times, in 2003, 2004, 2005 and 2010.
He scored in both the 2006 and 2009 Champions League finals, finding the net in each of Barcelona's triumphs.

footballers.name: Nani
clues: I won a European Championship and a Champions League.
I started out at Sporting Lisbon, the same academy that produced a far more famous countryman.
When I signed in England, many called me the natural heir to that countryman.
In one of the funniest moments in football, I tried to poke in a shot from that same countryman as it crossed the line, only for the goal to be ruled out because I was offside.
I loved to mark my goals with acrobatic somersaults.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 17th of November 1986. I played 112 times for my country, scoring 24 goals.
footballers.story: He arrived at Old Trafford as the boy from Sporting Lisbon carrying an impossible label, the next Cristiano Ronaldo, and for a while the stepovers and thunderbolts made you believe it. On his day Nani was pure theatre, a winger who could bend a free kick into the top corner then cartwheel away in celebration, and he collected four Premier League titles and the 2008 Champions League as United's dazzling wide threat. His career wandered on through Fenerbahce, Valencia, Lazio and Orlando, always with that flourish intact. But his defining night came in Paris in 2016, wearing the armband and lifting a trophy Portugal had never won.
didYouKnow: He joined Manchester United from Sporting Lisbon in 2007 and was billed as the heir to fellow Portuguese star Cristiano Ronaldo.
He wore the captain's armband in the Euro 2016 final after Ronaldo went off injured, leading Portugal to their first major trophy.
He was famous for his acrobatic somersault celebrations, flipping across the pitch after his biggest goals.

footballers.name: Rory Delap
clues: I cost Southampton a club-record fee of around 4 million pounds in 2001.
I was actually a midfielder, though almost nobody remembers me for what I did with my feet.
My son is now playing in the Premier League.
My club even narrowed their pitch to the minimum legal width to suit my game.
Opposing managers described my signature move as 'the best Scud missile I've ever seen' and 'a human sling'.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 6th of July 1976. I played 11 times for my country, without scoring.
footballers.story: Rory Delap turned the throw-in into a weapon of pure terror. A Carlisle-born midfielder who grew into a Premier League cult hero, he made his name with an arm honed on the javelin runway, launching flat, vicious deliveries that arrowed into the box like set-piece missiles. At Stoke City, opponents feared his hands more than most teams' free-kicks, some happily conceding a corner rather than let him load up. He gave the Britannia its snarl and Tony Pulis a tactic no defence could ever solve. Eleven caps for Ireland, and one unforgettable trademark.
footballers.numbers: 0 goals in 11 caps for Republic of Ireland
honours: Promotion to the Premier League (Stoke City, 2008)
didYouKnow: His long throw-ins were measured at close to 38 metres with a wickedly flat trajectory, and some Premier League sides preferred to concede a corner rather than give one away.
He was a county-champion javelin thrower as a schoolboy with a personal best around 55 metres, the discipline that shaped his trademark delivery.
His son Liam Delap became a Premier League striker with Chelsea, having grown up mimicking his father's fearsome long throw.

footballers.name: Fabio da Silva
clues: I am a Premier League winner and lost a Champions League final.
I moved to England as a teenager back in 2007.
I have an identical twin brother who was also a professional footballer.
Back home I won state titles with Gremio.
I could play at left-back or right-back with equal ease.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 9th of July 1990. I played 2 times for my country, without scoring.
footballers.story: For a few golden years at Old Trafford there were two of him, and even Sir Alex struggled to tell them apart. Fabio da Silva arrived from Fluminense in 2008 alongside his identical twin Rafael, a pair of buzzing Brazilian full-backs signed on the same day. Naturally two-footed, Fabio could raid down either flank, and he started the 2011 Champions League final against Barcelona at just 20. Injuries and the shadow of Patrice Evra meant United never quite became his stage, and later stops took in Cardiff, Middlesbrough and Nantes. Back home with Gremio, he finally settled into a steady groove.
didYouKnow: His identical twin brother Rafael joined Manchester United on the very same day in 2008 and played alongside him in the first team.
He started the 2011 Champions League final against Barcelona at Wembley, aged just 20.
Back home in Brazil he won back-to-back Campeonato Gaucho state titles with Gremio in 2023 and 2024.

footballers.name: Paolo Di Canio
clues: I began my career with the club I supported as a boy in my home city, before playing for several of Italy's grandest clubs.
In my first Scottish season I was voted the players' Player of the Year.
I once caught the ball instead of scoring into an empty net because the goalkeeper lay injured.
I scored a spectacular scissor-kick volley that was voted Goal of the Season.
That famous flying volley came in claret and blue, and West Ham fans adored me.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 9th of July 1968. I was never capped by my country.
footballers.story: Paolo Di Canio was football's beautiful contradiction, a mercurial forward who could conjure genius one moment and chaos the next. Born in Rome and raised on Lazio's terraces, he wandered through Juventus, Napoli and a title-winning AC Milan before finding his stage in Britain. At Celtic he was worshipped, voted the country's Player of the Year in a single electric season, and at West Ham he became a cult hero whose flair lit up Upton Park. Everything he did carried theatre, from his goal celebrations to his gestures of defiance and grace. He was maddening and magnificent, and for the fans who adored him, there was never a dull moment.
didYouKnow: His acrobatic scissor-kick volley against Wimbledon in March 2000 was voted the BBC's Goal of the Season.
Against Everton he caught the ball instead of scoring into an open goal because the keeper lay injured, an act that won him the FIFA Fair Play Award.
He remains a genuine cult hero at both Celtic and West Ham, adored for the flair and passion he brought to every match.

footballers.name: Marc Albrighton
clues: Early in my career my crossing drew some generous comparisons to David Beckham.
Aston Villa released me on a free transfer in 2014, which turned into one of the bargains of the decade.
I played in every one of my club's 38 league games during a title-winning season.
I scored my new club's first-ever goal in the Champions League, against Club Brugge.
I was a wide midfielder in the Leicester City side that won the Premier League at odds of 5000 to 1.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 18th of November 1989. I was never capped by my country at senior level.
footballers.story: An Aston Villa boy through and through, Marc Albrighton joined the claret-and-blue academy at eight and grew into a tricky, whip-crossing winger at Villa Park. Released on a free transfer in 2014, he made the short trip to Leicester and walked straight into the most improbable story in English football. When the 5000-1 outsiders lifted the Premier League in 2016, Albrighton was ever-present, gliding down the flank in all 38 games. He stayed a full decade, adding an FA Cup in 2021 and a Championship title in 2024. Ten years, honest graft, a quiet Foxes legend.
didYouKnow: He scored the Premier League's 20,000th goal for Aston Villa against Arsenal in December 2011, with the 20,000 pound prize donated to Acorns Children's Hospice.
He featured in every one of Leicester's 38 Premier League matches during their 2015-16 title-winning season.
He scored Leicester City's first ever Champions League goal, in a 3-0 win over Club Brugge in September 2016.

footballers.name: Leandro Paredes
clues: I have won a World Cup final.
Across my career I have played club football in four different countries.
At one club in France I lined up alongside Lionel Messi, Neymar and Kylian Mbappe.
I have disgraced myself in a World Cup final.
I am a boyhood fan and academy graduate of Boca Juniors.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 29th of June 1994. I played 84 times for my country, scoring 5 goals.
footballers.story: Leandro Paredes learned the game in the Boca Juniors youth ranks, a boyhood fan who grew up dreaming in blue and gold before ever wearing the shirt. From La Bombonera he carried his low centre of gravity and radar passing across Europe, dictating tempo at Roma, Zenit, Paris Saint-Germain and Juventus, always the man who slowed the game down so his teammates could speed up. Sitting deep in front of the defence, he became one of Argentina's quiet architects, threading the passes that let the forwards shine. Copa America glory in 2021 was the reward, and in Qatar he lifted the greatest prize of all. A metronome with a Boca heart, world champion at last.
didYouKnow: He is a 2022 World Cup winner and a two-time Copa America champion with Argentina, lifting the title in both 2021 and 2024.
A Boca Juniors boyhood fan, he came through the club's academy and made his professional debut for them before heading to Europe.
At Paris Saint-Germain he lined up alongside Lionel Messi, Neymar and Kylian Mbappe in one of the most star-studded midfields in the game.

footballers.name: Nuno Espirito Santo
clues: As a player I was an unused substitute on the bench as my club won a European final under Jose Mourinho.
I was the very first client signed by the super-agent Jorge Mendes.
I am currently a football manager in England.
I have taken two clubs from outside the Premier League's big six into European competition.
I managed Wolves, Tottenham, Nottingham Forest and then West Ham.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 25th of January 1974. I was never capped by my country.
footballers.story: Born in Sao Tome, Nuno Espirito Santo built his playing life as a goalkeeper who watched more than he played, a career of squad roles and reserve benches rather than headlines. On the night Jose Mourinho's Porto conquered Europe in the 2004 Champions League final, Nuno was an unused substitute, close enough to touch a dynasty without kicking a ball. But the dugout was where he truly belonged. He dragged Wolves out of the Championship and gave them Premier League swagger, then lifted Saudi Arabia's title with Al-Ittihad. The quiet understudy became one of the most respected managers of his generation.
didYouKnow: He was Jorge Mendes's very first client, meeting the future super-agent in the 1990s while still playing in goal.
He was an unused substitute on the Porto bench the night Jose Mourinho's side won the 2004 Champions League final.
A career goalkeeper by trade, he went on to become a Premier League manager with Wolves and Tottenham.

footballers.name: Ryan Bertrand
clues: I was named in the PFA Team of the Year for the 2014-15 season.
I made my Champions League debut by starting in the final itself, a game we won against a German giant.
I came through the academy at Chelsea, but had my best seasons on the south coast.
I played as a left-back.
I represented England at senior level.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 5th of August 1989. I played 19 times for my country, scoring 1 goal.
footballers.story: Ryan Bertrand was a Chelsea academy left-back who stumbled into folklore before most players get a sniff of the big time. Thrown into the 2012 Champions League final in Munich as a raw 22-year-old, he made his debut in the competition on the grandest night of all and walked off it a European champion. Life at Stamford Bridge never quite matched that opening chapter, but he found his true home on the south coast, anchoring Southampton's left flank for seven steady seasons and wearing the armband. Quick, dependable and rarely beaten one against one, he collected nineteen England caps before a late move to Leicester.
didYouKnow: He made his Champions League debut by starting the 2012 final against Bayern Munich, a match Chelsea went on to win on penalties.
He was named in the PFA Premier League Team of the Year for the 2014-15 season.
He spent seven seasons at Southampton, becoming a fixture at left-back and captaining the club.

footballers.name: Peter Odemwingie
clues: Since retiring as a footballer, I qualified as a PGA professional golfer.
On deadline day I drove to QPR expecting a transfer, and got filmed sitting in my car outside the ground.
My best years in England came as a forward for West Bromwich Albion.
My father is Nigerian and my mother is Russian, and I chose to play international football for Nigeria.
I also played up front for Stoke City.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 15th of July 1981. I played 65 times for my country, scoring 11 goals.
footballers.story: Born in Tashkent to a Nigerian father and a Russian mother, both of them medical students, Peter Odemwingie carried a wonderfully unlikely backstory into a well-travelled career. He made his name for Lille and Lokomotiv Moscow before West Bromwich Albion turned him into a Premier League favourite, a striker with a taste for the spectacular and a hat-trick at Wolves to treasure. Cardiff and Stoke followed, along with 65 caps for Nigeria and a decisive World Cup winner against Bosnia in 2014. He is remembered too for one chaotic deadline day, but there was always far more to his game than that famous drive.
didYouKnow: He was born in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, to a Nigerian father and a Russian mother who were both studying medicine there.
On transfer deadline day in January 2013 he filmed himself driving to QPR for a move that collapsed, leaving him stranded in his car outside Loftus Road.
After retiring from football he requalified as a PGA professional golfer, reaching the top level in a second sport.

footballers.name: Marek Hamsik
clues: I spent twelve seasons at one Italian club, becoming its record appearance-maker.
I overtook Diego Maradona to become my club's all-time record goalscorer.
I was part of the side that beat the reigning world champions to reach the last 16 on our World Cup debut as an independent nation.
I signed for Napoli from Brescia for just 5.5 million euros and stayed twelve years.
I was instantly recognisable for my distinctive mohawk haircut.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 27th of July 1987. I played 138 times for my country, scoring 26 goals.
footballers.story: For twelve seasons the mohawk was Napoli's heartbeat, a Slovak kid from Banska Bystrica who arrived from Brescia in 2007 and never wanted to leave. Hamsik ran the midfield with a driving elegance, arriving late in the box, threading passes no one else saw, and firing from distance when the mood took him. In December 2017 he swept past Diego Maradona to become Napoli's all-time leading scorer, a mortal outshining a god in that one column. Later chapters took him to Dalian and Trabzonspor, where a title finally came. But for Slovakia he stands alone: most caps, most goals, simply the greatest they have ever produced.
didYouKnow: In December 2017 he overtook Diego Maradona to become Napoli's all-time record goalscorer.
His towering mohawk became one of the most recognisable haircuts in world football.
He is Slovakia's most-capped player of all time, with 138 international appearances.

footballers.name: Richard Dunne
clues: I hold the outright record for the most own goals in Premier League history.
I captained Manchester City for several years in the 2000s.
I later played for Aston Villa and QPR after leaving Manchester City.
I helped the Republic of Ireland reach Euro 2012 with heroic defending.
I was the Manchester City captain remembered for both towering defending and a record number of own goals.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 21st of September 1979. I played 80 times for my country, scoring 8 goals.
footballers.story: Richard Dunne was the last line of defence made flesh, a big Dubliner who blocked, headed and threw his body across danger as if the goal behind him were his own front door. Everton gave him his start, but it was at Manchester City that he became a cult hero, wearing the armband and collecting the Player of the Year award four years running. Aston Villa and QPR followed, and everywhere he went he was loved for the same reasons: bravery, honesty and a total refusal to be beaten. For Ireland he was immense, never more so than the night in Moscow when he single-handedly frustrated Russia. Yes, he holds the record for Premier League own goals, but only a defender that committed puts himself in the firing line so often.
footballers.numbers: 8 goals in 80 caps for Republic of Ireland
didYouKnow: He holds the outright record for the most own goals in Premier League history, with ten.
He was named Manchester City's Player of the Year for four consecutive seasons, from 2005 to 2008.
His colossal display in a 0-0 draw away to Russia in 2011 earned him the nickname the Iron Curtain and helped Ireland reach Euro 2012.

footballers.name: Edinson Cavani
clues: I am one of my country's greatest ever scorers, but retired second on the list behind a famous teammate.
I scored both goals in a 2018 World Cup last-16 tie that knocked out Portugal and Cristiano Ronaldo.
I later spent time in the Premier League, wearing the number 7 shirt after arriving on a free transfer.
I was a league top scorer in Italy before moving to France for what was then a record fee for a French club.
I won six league titles in France with Paris Saint-Germain.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 14th of February 1987. I played 136 times for my country, scoring 58 goals.
footballers.story: They call him El Matador, and few forwards ever wore the name so honestly. Edinson Cavani ran the channels like a man chasing down a debt, all elbows and endless lungs, then finished with the calm of an assassin. He terrorised Serie A at Napoli, became the beating heart of Paris Saint-Germain's golden era, and even at Old Trafford, past 33, he still bent games to his will. For Uruguay he was the tireless partner to Suarez, second only to him in goals. Four World Cups, a Copa America, and not a single yard given for free.
didYouKnow: Cavani is Paris Saint-Germain's all-time leading goalscorer, netting 200 goals for the club between 2013 and 2020.
He was Serie A's top scorer in 2012-13, winning the Capocannoniere with 29 goals for Napoli.
He ranks as Uruguay's second-highest scorer of all time, behind only his long-time strike partner Luis Suarez.

footballers.name: Marc Overmars
clues: I won the Champions League in the 1990s, at the beginning of my career.
I was the most expensive winger in the world at one time.
Gary Neville named me the toughest winger he ever came up against in the Premier League.
I won the League and FA Cup Double in England in the 1997-98 season.
I scored a famous late winner at Old Trafford in March 1998 to lift my club's title bid.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 29th of March 1973. I played 86 times for my country, scoring 17 goals.
footballers.story: They called him the Flying Dutchman, and few nicknames ever fit so neatly. Marc Overmars came off Ajax's golden production line with a low centre of gravity and terrifying acceleration, lifting the Champions League in 1995 while barely into his twenties. Arsene Wenger brought that blur to Highbury, where Overmars flew down the left flank and powered Arsenal to the Double in 1998. A record move to Barcelona followed, and though the silverware dried up in Catalonia, the memory of his pace never did. Injuries tested him, but on his day he was simply unplayable.
footballers.numbers: 17 goals in 86 caps for the Netherlands
didYouKnow: He won the Champions League with Ajax in 1995, still only 21 when the young Dutch side beat AC Milan in the final.
His late winner at Old Trafford in March 1998 swung the title race Arsenal's way and helped seal their famous Double.
When he joined Barcelona in 2000 for around 25 million pounds, it was a then world-record fee for a winger and made him the most expensive Dutch player ever.

footballers.name: Paul Ince
clues: I began my career as a teenager at West Ham, the club I supported.
I won the European Cup Winners' Cup in 1991, and would go on to win two Premier League titles.
I was one of the few players to turn out for both Manchester United and Liverpool.
In 1995 I became the first Englishman in around 30 years to sign for Inter Milan, winning over the fans and reaching a UEFA Cup final.
I was the first black player to captain England's senior side, in 1993.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 21st of October 1967. I played 53 times for my country, scoring twice.
footballers.story: From the streets of Ilford to the roar of Old Trafford, Paul Ince played football like he owned it. A West Ham academy boy who anointed himself The Guv'nor, he became the snarling heartbeat of Alex Ferguson's first great Manchester United side, driving them to back-to-back titles with his shirt untucked and his chest out. In June 1993 he made history as the first black player to captain England, a moment bigger than any medal. He tested himself in Italy with Inter, then led the line at Liverpool, Boro and Wolves, forever competitive and forever loud. A born winner who never took a backward step.
didYouKnow: On 6 June 1993, in a friendly against the United States, Ince became the first black player to captain the England senior team.
He is one of very few players to have turned out for both Manchester United and Liverpool.
His self-styled nickname 'The Guv'nor' famously irritated Sir Alex Ferguson, who insisted there was only one guvnor at Old Trafford and it was not Ince.

footballers.name: Mikael Silvestre
clues: I once made a rare direct move between two fierce English rivals.
I began my professional career in France with Stade Rennais.
I was a versatile defender, equally at home at left-back or centre-back.
Across my years in England I collected four top-flight title medals.
I am one of the very few players to join Arsenal straight from Manchester United.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 9th of August 1977. I played 40 times for my country, scoring twice.
footballers.story: Mikael Silvestre was the quiet constant of Manchester United's back line, a Frenchman equally at home at left-back or centre-half, and Alex Ferguson trusted him to fill whichever gap the season demanded. He arrived from Inter Milan in 1999 after breaking through at Rennes, and stayed for nine years, racking up the medals as United piled up titles. He was never the household name alongside him, more the dependable understudy who rarely let the side down, and his finest afternoon came when he headed both goals to beat Liverpool. In 2008 he did the near-unthinkable, crossing the divide straight to Arsenal. For France he was a squad regular through the golden years, a World Cup finalist in 2006.
didYouKnow: A versatile left-back and centre-back, he won four Premier League titles and the 2008 Champions League with Manchester United.
He is one of very few players to move directly from Manchester United to Arsenal, switching sides in the summer of 2008.
A France international capped 40 times, he started out at Rennes before Inter Milan brought him to Italy as a teenager.

footballers.name: Victor Wanyama
clues: I was one of the first from my nation to star in British football.
I reached a Champions League final with a London club.
After England I crossed the Atlantic to play in MLS with a Montreal side.
I won league titles during my years in Scotland.
I once headed home the winning goal against Barcelona in the Champions League.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 25th of June 1991. I played 65 times for my country, scoring 8 goals.
footballers.story: Victor Wanyama was the great Kenyan trailblazer, the boy from Nairobi who kicked open doors and became one of the first from his country to truly matter in British football. Tall, powerful and deceptively composed, he was a defensive midfielder built for the modern game, breaking play up and driving it forward with equal appetite. He grew into a favourite at Celtic before Southampton made him a record signing and Tottenham handed him the biggest stage of all. Through it all he wore the Harambee Stars armband with pride, carrying a nation's hopes on broad shoulders. For millions of young Kenyans, he was living proof that the dream could reach Europe.
didYouKnow: He was Kenya's captain and one of the first Kenyan players to establish himself as a star in British football.
He scored the opening goal for Celtic in their famous 2-1 Champions League win over Barcelona in 2012.
He reached the 2019 Champions League final with Tottenham, who lost to Liverpool in Madrid.

footballers.name: Nigel Martyn
clues: I was a keen cricketer away from football.
I spent most of my international career as a back-up to an Arsenal legend.
When Crystal Palace signed me in 1989, I became the first one-million-pound goalkeeper in British football.
I saved a penalty on Sven-Goran Eriksson's very first night as England manager.
I kept goal for the Leeds side that reached a Champions League semi-final in 2001, and fans later voted me the club's greatest ever keeper.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 11th of August 1966. I played 23 times for my country, without scoring.
footballers.story: Nigel Martyn learned his trade on Cornwall's non-league fields before Bristol Rovers plucked him from obscurity. In 1989 he became Britain's first million-pound goalkeeper, a fee that felt absurd for a man between the sticks. At Crystal Palace he lifted a First Division title, then found his true home at Leeds United, where his shot-stopping made him a fixture in the side that reached a Champions League semi-final. For England he was the ultimate professional, steady and dependable, yet forever cast as understudy to David Seaman. Twenty-three caps hardly reflect his quality. He bowed out at Everton, still keeping clean sheets, still magnificent.
didYouKnow: His 1989 move from Bristol Rovers to Crystal Palace made him Britain's first million-pound goalkeeper.
He spent much of his England career as understudy to David Seaman, travelling to four major tournaments as backup.
Widely rated among Leeds United's finest keepers, he was the number one for the side that reached the 2001 Champions League semi-finals.

footballers.name: Mario Gomez
clues: A knee injury cost me a place in my country's 2014 World Cup winning squad.
I scored a penalty in a Champions League final shootout, but we lost.
My early breakthrough came at Stuttgart, though I won multiple Bundesliga titles with another German club.
I was a classic poacher, a natural finisher inside the box.
I spent time in Italy playing for Fiorentina.
footballers.kickoff: I was born on the 10th of July 1985. I played 78 times for my country, scoring 31 goals.
